10.17879/replicationresearch-2025-9022.laySummary: This editorial introduces Replication Research, an open-access journal dedicated to publishing studies that check whether previous scientific findings hold up when reanalyzed or repeated. The authors argue that science becomes more trustworthy when researchers value careful verification of previous discoveries as much as novel discoveries, but unfortunately replication studies still receive too little recognition. To address this, the journal aims to make replication research a more visible and respected part of the scientific process.

10.17879/replicationresearch-2026-10085.laySummary: Will we interpret a correlation correctly if we know about the "correlation is not causation" fallacy? This paper replicated a previous finding where a statement on top of a publication informed people about a wrong causal framing (X causes Y) in the study reporting a correlation (X and Y are related). The earlier authors found that when people read such a correction, they more often correctly interpreted correlations as an association and not as a causal finding. This study was able to replicate this result, also additionally showed that the finding holds even when changing small things about the analysis.

10.17879/replicationresearch-2026-9414.laySummary: In some situations, one may not want the reader of a text to know who the author is. This study repeated and extended a previous experiment on disguising a person's writing style to avoid author identification. It confirmed that changing writing style can make texts harder to attribute to their authors but found that the original study likely overstated the effect. The researchers also found machine translation as a surprisingly promising, if less effective, method for disguising a person's writing style.

10.17879/replicationresearch-2026-9577.laySummary: This editorial makes the point that researchers need to replicate more results from previous authors to build a good knowledge base of what is true or generalizable, but that is not enough: These replications also need to be seen and recognized more by the scientific community. The authors also argue that single replication studies of one specific effect are valuable and important, as they provide different information than so-called large-scale replications (where many authors replicate many effects and provide an overall estimate).
